paper.title: Internalizing Safety Understanding in Large Reasoning Models via Verification

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-7 and Appendices B (protocols, baselines, benchmarks, training details), C (extra preliminary results, proactive verification on other models, alternative specification); A (related work) and C.4 (case study) skimmed

claims.claim: A reasoning model's answers become safer, especially against jailbreak styles it was not trained on, if it is fine-tuned only to judge whether its own sampled answers to safety-relevant prompts violate a written safety specification, with an expert model's critique as the target, rather than fine-tuned to imitate safe answers. Supported only if, for three distilled reasoning models, this verification-only training gives lower attack success than both safe-answer distillation baselines (SafeChain, STAR-1) on every jailbreak benchmark not used to build the training data (Fortress, Jailbreak-R1) and on both reasoning-hijacking benchmarks (HCoT, Trotter); if compliance on benign but sensitive-sounding requests stays within 5 points of the untrained model and math accuracy within 2 points; and if the trained models judge the safety of the base model's answers with F1 at least 85, where answer-centric alignment leaves F1 near or below the base model's.
claims.decision_rule: SInternal ASR < SafeChain and < STAR-1 on Fortress, JailBreak-R1, HCoT, Trotter for DS-7B/8B/14B; XSTest CR >= base - 5; MATH >= base - 2; verification F1 >= 85 vs STAR-1/GRPO not clearly above base.

claims.claim: Verification training is a better starting point for reinforcement learning with safety rewards than safe-answer distillation or no initial fine-tuning: after the same RL run, the model started from verification training resists jailbreaks better, including attacks that hijack its reasoning, without refusing more. Supported only if, after identical GRPO training from each starting point on three models, the verification-trained start has the lowest attack success on Fortress in every model and is the only start below 70% success on the HCoT reasoning-hijack benchmark (others at 78% or more), while its compliance on benign sensitive requests is within 1 point of RL from the untrained model.
claims.decision_rule: After GRPO: SInternal Fortress ASR < all other starts on 3/3 models; HCoT ASR <= 64% vs >= 78% for all others; XSTest CR >= Base(+GRPO) - 1.

experiments.text: Define the training. Setup: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, -Llama-8B and -Qwen-14B. Seed prompts: 1k harmful and 1k benign sampled from WildJailbreak plus STAR-1's 1k harmful and 915 benign. For each prompt sample 8 responses from the model itself; Claude-4-Sonnet, given a bullet-point safety specification derived from common guardrail taxonomies, writes a critique and a safe/unsafe verdict for each; for harmful prompts keep only those with both safe and unsafe samples and use one of each, for benign prompts one trajectory (about 6,000 examples). LoRA fine-tuning (rank 16) to produce the critique and verdict given the specification, prompt and answer; the model is never trained on answers. RL stage: GRPO on the same safety prompts plus 3k DAPO math problems, Qwen3-Guard giving the safety and refusal reward (benign prompts rewarded only if safe and not refused).

Show that answer-centric alignment does not teach verification. Setup: WildJailbreak prompts answered by the base model, labelled by Llama-Guard-3-8B; ask models before and after SFT and RL alignment whether each answer meets the specification (F1 with unsafe as positive). Result: attack success falls through alignment while verification F1 does not improve: it degrades for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and hovers around the random baseline for -Qwen-7B (figure); the same holds with Qwen3Guard-8B as the labeller.

Compare with safe-answer distillation. Setup: SafeChain (about 20k vanilla harmful and benign samples, same training configuration) and STAR-1 (2k samples, two extra epochs); evaluation on StrongREJECT (direct harmful), WildJailbreak, Fortress and Jailbreak-R1 (jailbreaks), HCoT and Trotter (reasoning-hijack attacks), judged by Llama-Guard-3-8B as attack success; XSTest compliance judged by GPT-4o; MATH pass@1 and AIME pass@16. Result (7B / 8B / 14B): Fortress 22.6 / 18.6 / 19.2 against at best 33.2 / 26.2 / 28.2; Jailbreak-R1 11.8 / 6.1 / 1.3 against 15.3 / 9.3 / 5.1; HCoT 92 / 94 / 90 against 98-100; Trotter 19.7 / 26.3 / 33.3 against 29.8-49.0; StrongREJECT 7.0 / 1.6 / 0.6, worse than STAR-1 (2.9 / 0.0 / 0.6); XSTest 89.6 / 92.0 / 98.0 (base 90.8 / 96.0 / 95.6); MATH 88.4 / 84.4 / 89.6 (base 89.2 / 85.2 / 88.2).

Measure verification and its use during generation. Setup: F1 at judging the base model's answers with Claude-4-Sonnet labels; GPT-4o judges whether reasoning traces on WildJailbreak check the safety of the model's own intended behaviour; per-token KL divergence from the base model along harmful trajectories. Result: F1 85.9 / 89.0 / 89.3 after verification training, against 48.4 / 71.6 / 71.1 base, 32.2 / 59.3 / 53.9 after STAR-1 and 54.7 / 64.7 / 73.4 after GRPO (random 60-64). On DS-14B, self-verification appears in 50.4% of traces against 16.0% (base) and 28.4% (STAR-1), with 99.2% of those ending safely and 78.8% overall safety against 30.4% and 59.6%; on Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3-8B the gains over STAR-1 are small (48.4 vs 44.8%, 65.2 vs 64.8%). KL divergence stays higher deeper into harmful trajectories (figure).

Ablate what is learned from. Setup: swap verification data between DS-7B and DS-8B (each trained on the other's answers); drop the critique (verdict only) or the verdict (critique only) on DS-14B; replace the specification with Llama Guard 4's 14-category taxonomy; train on fractions of the data against a safe-answer SFT baseline. Result: own answers vs the other model's, ASR on StrongREJECT / Fortress / WildJailbreak 1.6 / 18.6 / 13.6 vs 3.8 / 20.4 / 19.6 (DS-8B) and 7.0 / 22.6 / 21.6 vs 9.6 / 27.4 / 27.6 (DS-7B); without critique 2.9 / 46.8 / 22.4 and without verdict 7.3 / 18.8 / 7.6 against 0.6 / 19.2 / 6.8; the alternative specification gives Fortress 21.0, WildJailbreak 6.8, XSTest 97.6; with 50% of the data it already beats the SFT baseline at full data (figure).

Note how the training data relates to the evaluations. Setup: verification training samples 2k prompts from WildJailbreak, while the baselines were restricted to vanilla harmful and benign prompts 'to study out-of-distribution jailbreaks', so WildJailbreak is not out of distribution for the proposed method; the expert critic (Claude-4-Sonnet), the RL reward model (Qwen3-Guard) and the evaluator (Llama-Guard-3-8B) differ, and on HCoT every untrained model and every distillation baseline already fails at or near 100%, so small differences there carry little weight. Results are single runs.

Run the same RL from each start. Setup: GRPO with identical hyperparameters and steps (64 prompts x 8 rollouts per batch) from the base model, SafeChain, STAR-1 and verification training. Result (7B / 8B / 14B): Fortress 11.0 / 2.8 / 5.2 against 17.0-25.2, 4.8-14.8 and 7.8-12.2; HCoT 64 / 38 / 62 against 96-98, 78-94 and 92-98; WildJailbreak 3.2 / 1.2 / 0.4 against at best 8.8 / 0.8 / 2.8 (STAR-1 start lower on 8B); Trotter 23.7 / 11.1 / 21.7, best on 8B and 14B, tied with the base start on 7B; XSTest 94.3 / 98.4 / 99.2 against 93.6 / 98.8 / 99.2 for the base start; MATH 89.8 / 84.2 / 89.6; AIME 83.3 / 60.0 / 80.0 against 80.0 / 66.7 / 80.0 for the base start.
